steps.explanationAfterStep: A Lewis base gives a pair, a Lewis acid takes it. Formal charges come from counting: nitrogen now shares its former lone pair, so it is positive; boron has gained a share in a pair, so it is negative. The molecule as a whole stays neutral.

title: Ammonia and boron trifluoride
subtitle: A Lewis acid–base adduct in one arrow
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 5 (Organic reactions)

reactants.caption: ammonia + boron trifluoride
hintTiers: Which molecule has a lone pair to give, and which has an atom with only six electrons around it?
Boron in BF₃ has an empty p orbital, so it can accept a pair without losing a bond. One arrow.
One arrow: the lone pair on ammonia's nitrogen to boron, making a new N–B bond.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Draw the arrow that joins ammonia to boron trifluoride.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Arrows start from electrons that move. Boron brings an empty orbital, not electrons, and its B–F bonds stay put. Start at nitrogen's lone pair.
Ammonia's nitrogen already has a full octet, so it cannot accept a new bond. Fluorine also holds its lone pairs very tightly. Find the atom that is short of electrons.

mechanismSummary: Nitrogen's lone pair, the source, forms a bond to boron, whose empty p orbital is the sink. No bond breaks, so one arrow is enough. Nitrogen ends with four bonds and a positive charge, boron with four bonds and a negative charge.
